CT4101 Topic Guide

Bayesian and Probabilistic Learning

Use prior belief and observed evidence to compare explanations — a lower-confidence CT4101 topic.

Exam-use protocol

Before writing, identify the command word: calculate/trace requires an ordered derivation; explain requires a definition, mechanism and assumption; compare/design requires matched criteria, a justified choice and a limitation. The topic-specific recall and worked routes below are the material to adapt—not text to copy blindly.

Part-by-part recall: definitions, assumptions and mechanics

Equation: P(H|E)=P(E|H)P(H)/P(E); Naive Bayes multiplies feature likelihoods conditional on class, an often imperfect conditional-independence assumption. Question cue: label prior, likelihood, evidence and posterior, then interpret uncertainty.

Worked practice 1 — paper-style synthesis (recurring-topic pattern; not a quoted paper prompt) Bayes

Question demand: Explain a posterior calculation. Plan/choice: write Bayes before numbers and normalise alternatives. Worked answer: multiply prior by class-conditional evidence for each class, divide by total evidence, choose/report the greater posterior. Mark-winning points: P(E) includes all hypotheses. Common trap: reverse P(E|H) and P(H|E).

Worked practice 2 — synthesis / design

Question demand: Use Naive Bayes for changing spam. Plan/choice: text features, smoothing, temporal validation and update. Worked answer: estimate class/word likelihoods with smoothing, retrain on recent labelled data and monitor drift/false positives; correlated words violate independence. Mark-winning points: assumption and mitigation. Common trap: unconditional independence.

Purpose and relevance

Bayesian learning expresses uncertainty with probabilities. It is useful when evidence is incomplete and when a classification decision should compare how likely evidence is under each class. Treat this as supporting revision: local evidence is older and it is not a strong prediction.

What a question really asks — answer plan

A Bayes question asks you to separate a base rate (prior) from evidence likelihood, calculate a posterior or compare unnormalised scores, then interpret the result in words.

Prerequisites, vocabulary and formulas

  • Bayes’ rule: P(C|E)=P(E|C)P(C)/P(E).
  • Prior P(C): belief before evidence; likelihood P(E|C): evidence probability if C is true; posterior P(C|E): updated belief.
  • For two classes, P(E)=P(E|C)P(C)+P(E|¬C)P(¬C).
  • Naive Bayes assumes features are conditionally independent given class, so P(x₁,…,xₙ|C)=ΠP(xᵢ|C).

Step-by-step method

  1. Define C and E, and copy supplied probabilities with their direction.
  2. Compute the evidence total P(E), if a posterior is required.
  3. Substitute into Bayes’ rule and give a decimal/percentage.
  4. For classification, compare P(C)ΠP(xᵢ|C) across classes; normalisation is unnecessary if only choosing the largest.

Worked practice 3 — foundational calculation

Question: P(D)=.10, P(+|D)=.90, P(+|¬D)=.05. Find P(D|+).

Model answer: P(+)=.90(.10)+.05(.90)=.135. Therefore P(D|+)=.90(.10)/.135=.667. A positive result raises probability to about 66.7%, not 90%, because the disease was initially uncommon and false positives exist.

Question interpretation and independent practice

Prompt 1

Is P(+|D) the same as P(D|+)? Check: no: the first is likelihood/sensitivity; the second is posterior. Bayes’ rule connects them.

Exam bridge

Explain Naive Bayes, state its assumption, and show how to classify a record with two categorical features. Check: compute a prior-times-likelihood-product score per class, choose larger, and explicitly call the conditional-independence assumption a simplifying assumption that may be imperfect.

High-value traps and corrections

Paper basis for the integrated practice: syllabus/concept practice. The local archive was checked, but this diagnostic-posterior scenario is not claimed as a direct paper adaptation.

Integrated syllabus-based practice - diagnostic posterior [8 marks]

Scenario. P(D)=.10, P(+|D)=.90 and P(+|not D)=.05. Calculate P(D|+) and explain why a positive does not mean 90% disease probability.

Question-demand diagnosis: distinguish likelihood from posterior and include base rate.

Fastest route: calculate P(+)=.90(.10)+.05(.90)=.135, then divide .09 by it.

Worked answer: P(D|+)=.09/.135=.667. The likelihood is 90%, but disease is initially uncommon and false positives contribute .045 to all positive tests. The posterior therefore rises substantially but is not 90%. In a classifier, report uncertainty and decision costs rather than treating this posterior as a diagnosis.

Topic-specific trap: P(+|D) and P(D|+) have different conditions.

  • Reversing P(E|C) and P(C|E).
  • Ignoring the base rate.
  • Claiming features are unconditionally independent in Naive Bayes.

Final answer checklist

  • Have I labelled each conditional probability?
  • Did I calculate P(E) when needed?
  • Did I interpret the posterior rather than only report it?

Bayesian/Naive Bayes material is mainly supported by local 2019/20 evidence and is lower confidence than CT4101’s core current topics. Cover it after the higher-confidence guides; do not infer likely order or appearance.
